• Gelatin and Pectin

  • become thick and firm.

questions.question: Define JECFA and CAC.
questions.solution_html:
• Define JECFA and CAC. / [CO1]
  • JECFA
  • JECFA is an independent scientific committee created by the Food and Agriculture
  • Organization (FAO) and the World Health Organization (WHO). JECFA decides
  • whether a food additive is safe and how much of it can be safely eaten.
  • Main functions:
  • • Evaluates the safety of food additives, contaminants, and residues.
  • • Conducts risk assessments based on scientific studies.
  • • Establishes Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI) values, which indicate how much of a
  • substance can be safely consumed daily over a lifetime.
  • CAC
  • The Codex Alimentarius Commission was also established by FAO and WHO.
  • Main functions:
  • • Develops international food standards, guidelines, and codes of practice.
  • • Creates the General Standard for Food Additives (GSFA), which lists:
  • • Approved food additives
  • • Maximum permitted levels in different foods
  • • Helps protect consumer health and ensures fair food trade worldwide.

questions.question: Describe the method used to measure thickness using a micrometer. [5x4 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the method used to measure thickness using a micrometer. / [CO3]
  • Thickness is the distance between the two surfaces of paper, paperboard, or flexible packaging
  • material.
  • Method of Test: (Equipment name : micrometer)
  • • Cut a specimen of 10 cm × 10 cm.
  • • Place it between the two anvils of a micrometer.
  • • Gently lower the upper anvil and note the reading.
  • • Take at least 10 readings and calculate the average.
  • • Thickness is expressed in micron, inches, mil, or gauge.

questions.question: List out the properties of food additives.
questions.solution_html:
• List out the properties of food additives. / [CO1]
  • Preservation
  • • Preservation is one of the most important functions of food additives. Preservatives
  • extend the shelf life of foods by inhibiting the growth of spoilage and microorganisms
  • such as bacteria, yeasts and molds. Eg: potassium sorbate and sodium benzoate are
  • commonly used in beverages, sauces, pickles and bakery products to inhibit molds
  • and yeasts.
  • • In addition to microbial control, oxidation (fat react with oxygen to form off-flavour
  • amnd off-odour) is another major cause of food spoilage.
  • Antioxidants such as ascorbic acid (vitamin C) prevent oxidation of fats and oils.
  • Sensory Enhancement
  • • Taste enhancement: Flavouring agents and acids improve palatability (how tasty food
  • is). Monosodium glutamate (MSG) is a flavour enhancer that intensifies umami taste
  • in soups, sauces and processed foods
  • • Appearance (colour): Colour additives restore or enhance the natural colour lost
  • during processing. Natural colours such as carotenoids, annatto, and chlorophyll.
  • • Texture modification: Emulsifiers like lecithin and mono- and diglycerides help in
  • uniform mixing of oil and water in products such as mayonnaise and margarine.
  • Thickeners and stabilizers such as pectin, guar gum and carrageenan improve
  • viscosity, mouthfeel and consistency in sauces, jams and ice cream.
  • • Aroma enhancement: Flavouring substances contribute characteristic aromas, for
  • example vanilla in bakery products or fruit esters in beverages. (smell)
  • Nutritional Enhancement
  • • Food additives play an important role in improving the nutritional quality of foods
  • through fortification. Vitamins such as vitamin A, D and B-complex are added to
  • milk, flour and cereals to prevent deficiency diseases. Minerals like iron, calcium and
  • iodine are incorporated into salt, flour and beverages
  • Processing Aids
  • • Leavening agents, such as baking powder and baking soda, release carbon dioxide
  • during baking, causing dough expansion and producing soft, porous bakery products.
  • • Anti-caking agents like silicon dioxide and calcium silicate prevent clumping in
  • powdered foods such as salt, sugar and spice mixes.
  • • Enzymes used in food processing also fall under processing aids, improving
  • efficiency and product quality. (ptns that speed up chemical reactions)
  • Safety and Stability
  • • Food additives must be safe for human consumption and stable under processing and
  • storage conditions.
  • • Stability ensures that additives do not break down into harmful substances when
  • exposed to heat, light or oxygen.

questions.question: Classify preservatives into Class I and Class II along with their functions, examples, and permitted levels.
questions.solution_html: • Classify preservatives into Class I and Class II along with their functions, examples, and permitted levels. / [CO2] A preservative is defined as any substance which is capable of inhibiting, retarding, or arresting, the growth of micro -organisms, of any deterioration of food due to micro - organisms, or of masking the evidence of any such deterioration. Class I preservatives are natural substances and can be used without restriction e.g. salt, sugar, spices, vinegar. Sodium chloride : Salts stop the growth of microorganisms and interfere with the action of proteolytic enzymes. Salts also cause food dehydration by drawing out water from the tissue cells. Used in butter, cheese, cabbage, olives, cucumbers, meat, fish and bread. Sugar: Sugar acid in the preservation of products in which it is used. The high osmotic pressure of sugar creates conditions that are unfavourable for the growth and reproduction of most species of bacteria, yeasts and molds. Used in syrups and confectionary products, fondant fillings in chocolate, honey, jellies, marmalades, conserves and fruits such as dates, sultanas and currants. Class II preservatives are man made and their use is restricted to only certain foods and the amount of the preservative which can be added to these foods is also specified under PFA rules. Preservative E Number Food Applications Permitted Level* Main Function Sulfur dioxide E220- E228 Treatment of fruits & vegetables before and after dehydration; storage of fresh grapes; wine making; manufacture of fruit juices; dried fruits; cut fruits 50–2000 mg/kg depending on food Extends storage life; prevents growth of undesirable microorganisms and prevents browning reactions; Sorbic acid E200– E203 Cheese, baked products, fruit juices, wines, pickles Up to 1000 mg/kg Inhibits moulds and yeasts Acetic acid E260– E263 Pickled vegetables; bread and baked foods; mayonnaise and pickles GMP Prevents ropiness and mould growth Propionic acid E280– E283 Bakery products Up to 2000– 3000 mg/kg Inhibits moulds; active against ropy bread organism Bacillus mesentericus Benzoic acid E210– E213 Fruit juices, carbonated beverages, pickles, sauerkraut Up to 1000 mg/kg Antimicrobial; most active against yeasts and bacteria Parabens E214– E219 General food preservation Up to 300 mg/kg Effective inhibitors of moulds and yeasts; relatively ineffective against bacteria. Ethylene oxide & Propylene oxide —- Dry items such as nuts and spices Not permitted directly in foods; only for fumigation of certain dry foods under strict regulation Destroy all forms of microorganisms including spores and viruses

questions.question: Explain the concept of intelligent packaging and describe the different types of indicators used in it. [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the concept of intelligent packaging and describe the different types of
  • indicators used in it. / [CO3]
  • Intelligent packaging is defined as packaging that contains an external or internal indicator to
  • provide information about aspects of the history of the package and/or the quality of the food.
  • External indicators are those indicators which are attached outside the package like time -
  • temperature indicators
  • Internal indicators are those indicators which are placed inside the package, either to the head-
  • space of the package or attached into the lid like oxygen indicators for indication of oxygen or
  • package leak, carbon dioxide indicators, microbial growth indicators and pathogen indicators
  • Various examples of internal and external indicators are shown in the table below:
  • Time–Temperature Indicators (TTIs)
  • Time–Temperature Indicators record the temperature history of packaged foods during storage,
  • transport, and sale. They provide information about food quality and safety through irreversible
  • changes. TTIs are classified into diffusion, microbial, enzyme, polymerization, and light color
  • types. They are mainly used for temperature-sensitive foods such as frozen and chilled foods.
  • Freshness Indicators
  • Freshness indicators show the freshness of food by detecting metabolites produced during
  • spoilage. These indicators often produce visible color changes when reacting with compounds
  • such as glucose, organic acids, ethanol, volatile nitrogen compounds, CO₂, sulfides, and
  • biogenic amines. They are commonly used for fresh foods like fruits and seafood.
  • Leak Indicators
  • Leak indicators detect changes in gas composition inside food packages caused by respiration,
  • microbial activity, or package leakage. They help monitor food quality and safety . Common
  • gases detected include oxygen (O₂) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) , while others like water vapor,
  • ethanol, and hydrogen sulfide may also be monitored.
  • pH Indicators
  • pH indicators detect changes in pH levels of packaged foods . Natural compounds such as
  • anthocyanins (polyphenols) are commonly used because they change color with pH variations,
  • indicating food spoilage.
